::: {.callout-note icon="true"}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- explain why repeated `SEQN` values require investigation;
- distinguish duplicates within one source from overlap across sources;
- compare the 2001–2002 primary and second CBC examinations;
- identify participants appearing in both files;
- distinguish exact duplicate rows from different measurements;
- preserve the second examination as supplementary data;
- create duplicate-audit reports;
- prepare a clean set of primary CBC sources for combination.
:::

## Why duplicate handling matters

A duplicate participant key is not automatically an error.

Repeated identifiers can represent:

- an exact duplicate row;
- a repeat examination;
- a second specimen;
- a complementary record;
- conflicting values;
- a source with more than one row per participant;
- the same participant appearing in more than one source file.

Deleting repeated records without understanding their meaning can remove scientifically valuable information.

## The specific issue in this pipeline

The 2001–2002 CBC release contains two relevant files:

```text
L25_B
L25_2_B
```

In this tutorial:

- `L25_B` is treated as the primary CBC examination;
- `L25_2_B` is treated as a supplementary second examination.

Some participants may appear in both files.

Appending both files directly into one primary person-level dataset would create repeated participant-cycle keys.

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Do not use this shortcut

```r
dplyr::distinct(
  SEQN,
  .keep_all = TRUE
)
```

This keeps one arbitrary row and discards the others.

It does not determine whether the discarded records are:

- exact copies;
- repeat measurements;
- complementary observations;
- conflicting observations.
:::

## Check duplicates within each individual file

Create a helper function:

```r
find_duplicate_keys <- function(
    data,
    key_columns) {

  data |>
    dplyr::count(
      dplyr::across(
        dplyr::all_of(
          key_columns
        )
      ),
      name = "occurrences"
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(
      occurrences > 1
    )
}
```

Check the primary file:

```r
primary_internal_duplicates <- find_duplicate_keys(
  data = cbc_2001_2002_primary,
  key_columns = "SEQN"
)
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  primary_internal_duplicates,
  n = Inf
)
```

Check the second examination:

```r
second_exam_internal_duplicates <- find_duplicate_keys(
  data = cbc_2001_2002_second_exam,
  key_columns = "SEQN"
)
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  second_exam_internal_duplicates,
  n = Inf
)
```

These checks answer:

```text
Does one source file contain repeated SEQN values internally?
```

They do not yet answer whether the same participant appears across both files.

## Identify participants appearing in both files

Create one distinct key table for each source:

```r
primary_participants <- cbc_2001_2002_primary |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    survey_cycle,
    SEQN
  )
```

```r
second_exam_participants <- cbc_2001_2002_second_exam |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    survey_cycle,
    SEQN
  )
```

Find shared participants:

```r
shared_second_exam_participants <- primary_participants |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    second_exam_participants,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    SEQN
  )
```

Count them:

```r
nrow(
  shared_second_exam_participants
)
```

This is the number of participants who have both:

- a primary CBC examination;
- a second CBC examination.

## Identify participants found only in the primary file

Run:

```r
primary_only_participants <- primary_participants |>
  dplyr::anti_join(
    second_exam_participants,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  )
```

Count:

```r
nrow(
  primary_only_participants
)
```

## Identify participants found only in the second examination

Run:

```r
second_exam_only_participants <- second_exam_participants |>
  dplyr::anti_join(
    primary_participants,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  )
```

Count:

```r
nrow(
  second_exam_only_participants
)
```

::: {.callout-important icon="true"}
## A second-exam-only participant is not automatically an error

A participant appearing only in the supplementary source may reflect:

- source eligibility;
- missing primary results;
- release structure;
- a valid follow-up record;
- a source-specific inclusion rule.

Preserve and report such records rather than deleting them.
:::

## Separate metadata from scientific variables

The imported datasets contain metadata columns added by the pipeline.

Define them:

```r
source_metadata_columns <- c(
  "survey_cycle",
  "source_dataset_id",
  "source_component",
  "source_file_id",
  "source_exam",
  "analysis_role",
  "source_url",
  "local_source_file",
  "source_sha256"
)
```

Identify common scientific variables:

```r
common_scientific_variables <- setdiff(
  common_second_exam_variables,
  source_metadata_columns
)
```

Ensure `SEQN` is included:

```r
if (
  !"SEQN" %in%
    common_scientific_variables
) {
  stop(
    "SEQN is not available in both CBC sources."
  )
}
```

## Join shared participants for comparison

Add suffixes so primary and second-exam values can be compared side by side:

```r
shared_second_exam_comparison <-
  cbc_2001_2002_primary |>
  dplyr::semi_join(
    shared_second_exam_participants,
    by = c(
      "survey_cycle",
      "SEQN"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    dplyr::all_of(
      common_scientific_variables
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    cbc_2001_2002_second_exam |>
      dplyr::semi_join(
        shared_second_exam_participants,
        by = c(
          "survey_cycle",
          "SEQN"
        )
      ) |>
      dplyr::select(
        dplyr::all_of(
          common_scientific_variables
        )
      ),
    by = "SEQN",
    suffix = c(
      "_primary",
      "_second"
    )
  )
```

Inspect:

```r
dplyr::glimpse(
  shared_second_exam_comparison
)
```

## Why compare only shared variables?

A row cannot be classified as an exact duplicate when the two source schemas differ unless comparison is restricted to variables available in both sources.

Even then, identical values across common variables do not prove that the two source files are conceptually interchangeable.

The source role must still be preserved.

## Build a value-comparison function

Create:

```r
values_equal_with_missing <- function(
    first_value,
    second_value) {

  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(first_value) &
      is.na(second_value) ~ TRUE,

    is.na(first_value) |
      is.na(second_value) ~ FALSE,

    TRUE ~ first_value ==
      second_value
  )
}
```

## Identify comparable measurement variables

Remove `SEQN` from the comparison variables:

```r
measurement_variables <- setdiff(
  common_scientific_variables,
  "SEQN"
)
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  measurement_variables
)
```

## Compare each shared participant across common variables

Create a long comparison table:

```r
shared_measurement_comparison <-
  purrr::map_dfr(
    measurement_variables,
    function(variable_name) {

      primary_column <- paste0(
        variable_name,
        "_primary"
      )

      second_column <- paste0(
        variable_name,
        "_second"
      )

      tibble::tibble(
        SEQN =
          shared_second_exam_comparison$SEQN,
        variable =
          variable_name,
        primary_value =
          shared_second_exam_comparison[[
            primary_column
          ]],
        second_exam_value =
          shared_second_exam_comparison[[
            second_column
          ]],
        values_match =
          values_equal_with_missing(
            shared_second_exam_comparison[[
              primary_column
            ]],
            shared_second_exam_comparison[[
              second_column
            ]]
          )
      )
    }
  )
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  shared_measurement_comparison,
  n = 50
)
```

## Summarize differences by variable

Run:

```r
second_exam_variable_difference_summary <-
  shared_measurement_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    variable
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    compared_participants =
      dplyr::n(),
    matching_values =
      sum(
        values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    different_values =
      sum(
        !values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    percent_different =
      100 *
      different_values /
      compared_participants,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    dplyr::desc(
      different_values
    ),
    variable
  )
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  second_exam_variable_difference_summary,
  n = Inf
)
```

Variables with different values provide evidence that the second examination contains distinct measurements rather than simple duplicate copies.

## Classify each shared participant

Create a participant-level summary:

```r
second_exam_participant_comparison <-
  shared_measurement_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    SEQN
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    compared_variables =
      dplyr::n(),
    matching_variables =
      sum(
        values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    different_variables =
      sum(
        !values_match,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
    all_common_values_match =
      all(
        values_match
      ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    comparison_class =
      dplyr::case_when(
        all_common_values_match ~
          "all_common_values_match",

        different_variables > 0 ~
          "different_measurements",

        TRUE ~
          "unresolved"
      )
  )
```

Inspect:

```r
print(
  second_exam_participant_comparison,
  n = Inf
)
```

## Interpret the comparison classes

### `all_common_values_match`

All compared common values are identical.

This is evidence of a value-level match across the shared variables.

It does not justify deleting the supplementary source because:

- source roles differ;
- source provenance differs;
- nonshared variables may differ;
- the records belong to separate examination contexts.

### `different_measurements`

At least one common variable differs between the primary and second examinations.

This indicates that the second record contains distinct measurements.

### `unresolved`

The comparison could not be classified completely.

This category should be preserved and investigated.

## Extract matched participants

Run:

```r

primary_cbc_cycle_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(

    tibble::tibble(

```

## Why the second examination is not discarded

The second examination remains valuable for:

- repeat-measurement analysis;
- within-person comparison;
- measurement stability;
- quality-control investigation;
- methodological research;
- sensitivity analyses.

Its exclusion from the primary stack is an analytical design decision, not a judgment that the data are invalid.

## Why source roles must remain explicit

The following two statements are different:

```text
This row is a duplicate.
```

```text
This participant has a second examination.
```

The first implies redundancy.

The second describes study design.

The pipeline preserves that distinction through:

```text
source_exam
analysis_role
source_file_id
inclusion_in_primary_stack
```

## Common mistakes

### Appending `L25_B` and `L25_2_B`

This creates repeated participant-cycle keys in the main CBC stack.

### Deleting the second examination

This loses scientifically useful repeat-measurement data.

### Using `distinct(SEQN, .keep_all = TRUE)`

This keeps an arbitrary record without scientific justification.

### Comparing every column directly

Pipeline metadata and source-specific variables may differ even when scientific measurements match.

### Calling all shared participants exact duplicates

The same participant appearing in both files does not mean the measurement values are identical.

### Treating identical common values as proof of redundancy

Identical values across shared variables do not erase differences in source role, examination context, or nonshared variables.

- [ ] The second examination was saved separately.
- [ ] The primary CBC source list contains 10 files.
- [ ] The supplementary source is excluded from the primary list.
- [ ] Each cycle has exactly one primary CBC source.
- [ ] Duplicate-audit reports were saved.

## Knowledge check

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why should `L25_2_B` not be appended to the primary CBC stack?

It represents a second examination for participants who may already appear in `L25_B`. Appending it would create repeated participant-cycle keys and mix primary and repeat measurements.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Does a shared `SEQN` prove that two rows are exact duplicates?

No. It proves only that the same participant appears in both sources. Measurement values and source context must still be compared.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why preserve the second examination?

It may support repeat-measurement, reliability, quality-control, and methodological analyses even though it is excluded from the main primary stack.
:::

## Lesson summary

You have:

- investigated duplicate keys within the two 2001–2002 CBC sources;
- identified participants shared across examinations;
- compared common measurements;
- classified matched, different, and unresolved records;
- preserved the second examination separately;
- created a clean list of 10 primary CBC sources;
- saved a complete duplicate-audit trail.
